claims.claim: Modernity has traditionally been presented in philosophical and sociological literature as an age where artifacts supplant nature and destroy the natural environment through a process of de-naturalization, a view questioned by Hannah Arendt who argues that re-naturalization has been taking place to the detriment of the human world.
qualifications: applies to the centuries of the modern age
claims.supporting_excerpt: Modernity, in philosophical and sociological literature, has “traditionally” been presented as the age when artifacts supplant nature and destroy the originally given natural environment. The process of modernization, from this point of view, is the process of de-naturalization . This widely shared conviction has ba - sically been questioned by Hannah Arendt. During the centuries of modern age, in the detriment of the commonly created and uphold human world, process of re-naturalization  has been taking place, Arendt argues.

claims.claim: Arendt transformed the interpretation of the natural-artificial dichotomy inherited from German cultural criticism by subordinating the ecological connotations to the requirements of her political philosophy centered on plurality and liberty.
qualifications: framed as author's hypothesis regarding Arendt's work
claims.supporting_excerpt: It is my initial hypothesis that Arendt transformed the interpretation of this dichotomy inherited from the German cultural criticism... the ecological connotations of natural–artificial  dichotomy, in The Human Condition, were subordinated to the requirements of her political philosophy.

definitions.definition: The process where artifacts supplant nature and destroy the originally given natural environment.
A process taking place during the modern age to the detriment of the commonly created and upheld human world, enhanced by technology.

distinctions.distinction: The Arendtian critique of modernity takes a difference between the notions of Earth and world.

must_not_be_lost: Arendt's interpretation of natural and artificial in The Human Condition is tied to two narratives: cultural criticism and political philosophy.
Arendt's thought was influenced by inter-war German cultural criticism and Martin Heidegger's philosophy.
